body: In the department of... but it is better not to say which department. There is nothing more touchy than every kind of department, regiment, government office and, in a word, every kind of official body. Nowadays every private person considers the whole of society insulted in his own person. They say that quite recently a petition came in from a certain district police chief, I don’t remember of which town, in which he set out clearly that the laws of the state were perishing and that his sacred name was being taken absolutely in vain. And as proof he attached to his petition an enormous volume of some romantic work in which, every ten pages, a district police chief appears, in places even completely drunk. And so, to avoid any unpleasantness, we had better call the department in question a certain department. And so, in a certain department there served a certain clerk; a clerk who could not be called very remarkable: short, somewhat pockmarked, somewhat reddish-haired, even somewhat short-sighted to look at, with a small bald patch on his forehead, wrinkles on both cheeks, and the kind of complexion that is called haemorrhoidal... What can one do! The Petersburg climate is to blame. As for his rank (for with us the rank must be announced first of all), he was what is called an eternal titular councillor, a low rank which, as everyone knows, has been mocked and jeered at to their hearts’ content by various writers who have the praiseworthy habit of attacking those who cannot bite back. The clerk’s surname was Bashmachkin. From the very name it is clear that it once came from *bashmak*, a shoe; but when, at what time and in what way it came from a shoe, nothing of that is known. His father, his grandfather and even his brother-in-law, and absolutely all the Bashmachkins, went about in boots, having them resoled only three times a year. His name was Akaky Akakievich. Perhaps it will seem to the reader somewhat strange and far-fetched, but one can assure him that it was not looked for at all, but that circumstances arose of their own accord which made it quite impossible to give him any other name; and this is exactly how it happened. Akaky Akakievich was born towards night, if memory does not deceive, on the 23rd of March. His late mother, a clerk’s wife and a very good woman, arranged, as is proper, to have the child christened. His mother was still lying in bed facing the door, and on her right stood the godfather, a most excellent man, Ivan Ivanovich Yeroshkin, who served as head clerk in the Senate, and the godmother, the wife of a district police officer, a woman of rare virtues, Arina Semyonovna Belobryushkova. The mother was offered her choice of any of three names: Mokkius, Sossius, or naming the child after the martyr Khozdazat. “No,” thought the late lady, “those are all such names.” To please her, they opened the church calendar at another place; out came three names again: Trifily, Dula and Varakhasy. “What a punishment,” said the old woman, “what names they all are; I really have never heard such names. Varadat or Varukh, perhaps, but Trifily and Varakhasy!” They turned another page, and out came: Pavsikakhy and Vakhtisy. “Well, I see,” said the old woman, “that this must be his fate. If so, better let him be called after his father. His father was Akaky, so let the son be Akaky too.” And that is how Akaky Akakievich came about. The child was christened, and during it he cried and made such a face as if he foresaw that he would be a titular councillor. So that is how it all came about. We have told this so that the reader can see for himself that it happened entirely out of necessity, and that it was quite impossible to give him any other name. When and at what time he entered the department, and who appointed him, nobody could remember. However many directors and chiefs of every kind changed, he was always seen in one and the same place, in the same position, in the same post, the same copying clerk, so that people became convinced at last that he must have been born into the world already completely ready, in uniform and with a bald patch on his head. In the department no respect at all was shown him. The porters not only did not get up from their seats when he passed, but did not even glance at him, as if a simple fly had flown through the waiting room. His superiors treated him in a sort of coldly despotic way. Some assistant head clerk would shove papers right under his nose without even saying “copy this”, or “here is an interesting, nice little piece of work”, or anything pleasant, as is customary in well-mannered offices. And he would take it, looking only at the paper, without looking to see who had put it there or whether he had the right to. He would take it and at once settle down to copy it. The young clerks laughed and made jokes at him, as far as their office wit allowed, told all sorts of stories about him in front of him, invented about him; they said his landlady, an old woman of seventy, beat him; they asked when their wedding would be; they scattered bits of paper on his head and called it snow. But Akaky Akakievich answered not a word, as if there were no one in front of him; it did not even affect his work: amid all this pestering he did not make a single mistake in his copying. Only if the joke was too unbearable, when they jogged his arm and kept him from his work, would he say: “Leave me alone; why do you insult me?” And there was something strange in the words and in the voice in which they were spoken. Something in it moved one to pity, so much so that one young man, newly appointed, who, following the example of the others, had allowed himself to make fun of him, suddenly stopped as if pierced, and from then on everything seemed to change before him and appear in a different light. Some unnatural force pushed him away from the colleagues he had got to know, taking them for decent, well-bred people. And long afterwards, in the midst of his gayest moments, there would appear to him the little clerk with the bald patch on his forehead, with his piercing words: “Leave me alone; why do you insult me?”, and in those piercing words rang other words: “I am your brother.” And the poor young man would cover his face with his hand, and many times afterwards in his life he shuddered, seeing how much inhumanity there is in man, how much savage coarseness is hidden in refined, educated good manners, and, God! even in a man whom the world regards as noble and honourable...

It would be hard to find a man anywhere who lived so in his work. It is not enough to say that he served zealously; no, he served with love. There, in this copying, he saw a varied and pleasant world of his own. Delight showed in his face; certain letters were his favourites, and when he came to them he was beside himself: he chuckled and winked and helped with his lips, so that one could, it seemed, read in his face every letter his pen was forming. If he had been rewarded in proportion to his zeal, he might, to his own astonishment, have even become a state councillor; but all he earned, as his witty colleagues put it, was a buckle in his buttonhole and piles in his backside. However, it cannot be said that no attention was paid to him at all. One director, being a kind man and wishing to reward him for his long service, ordered that he be given something more important than ordinary copying: he was told to draw up, from a case already completed, a letter to another government office; all it involved was changing the heading and changing some of the verbs from the first person to the third. This gave him so much work that he broke into a sweat, rubbed his forehead and finally said: “No, better let me copy something.” From then on they left him to copy for ever. Outside this copying, nothing seemed to exist for him. He gave no thought at all to his clothes: his uniform was not green but some sort of rusty floury colour. Its collar was narrow and low, so that his neck, although it was not long, seemed extraordinarily long as it came out of the collar, like those plaster kittens with nodding heads that foreigners carry on their heads by the dozen to sell in Russia. And something was always sticking to his uniform: a wisp of hay, or a bit of thread; besides, he had a special knack, when walking in the street, of passing under a window just as some rubbish was being thrown out of it, and so he was forever carrying away melon and watermelon rinds and such nonsense on his hat. Not once in his life did he pay attention to what was happening and going on every day in the street, which, as everyone knows, his fellow young clerk will always look at, carrying the sharpness of his lively gaze so far that he will even notice whose trouser strap has come undone at the bottom on the other side of the pavement, which always brings a sly grin to his face.

But Akaky Akakievich, if he looked at anything at all, saw on everything his own clean lines, written in an even hand; and only if, coming from heaven knows where, a horse’s muzzle came to rest on his shoulder and blew a whole wind from its nostrils onto his cheek, only then did he notice that he was not in the middle of a line but rather in the middle of the street. When he got home he sat down at once at the table, hastily gulped his cabbage soup and ate a piece of beef with onion, without noticing their taste at all; he ate it all with the flies and with whatever else God sent at the time. Noticing that his stomach was beginning to swell, he would get up from the table, take out his bottle of ink and copy the papers he had brought home. If there were none, he would make a copy for himself, on purpose, for his own pleasure, especially if the paper was remarkable not for the beauty of its style but for being addressed to some new or important person.

Even in those hours when the grey Petersburg sky has gone quite dark and all the clerkly folk have eaten and dined, each as he could, according to the salary he received and his own fancy; when everyone has rested after the scratching of pens in the department, the running about, their own and other people’s necessary business, and all that restless man voluntarily sets himself, even more than is necessary; when the clerks hurry to give the rest of their time to pleasure: the livelier one rushes to the theatre; another to the street, to spend it looking at ladies’ little hats; another to an evening party, to waste it on compliments to some pretty girl, the star of a small clerkly circle; another, and this happens most often, simply goes to see his fellow clerk on the fourth or third floor, in two little rooms with a hall or a kitchen and some pretensions to fashion, a lamp or some other knick-knack that cost many sacrifices, going without dinners and outings; in a word, even at the time when all the clerks scatter to the little flats of their friends to play a stormy game of whist, sipping tea from glasses with kopeck rusks, drawing smoke from long pipes, and telling, while the cards are dealt, some gossip carried down from high society, which a Russian can never give up in any condition, or even, when there is nothing to talk about, retelling the eternal anecdote about the commandant who was told that the tail of the horse on Falconet’s monument had been cut off; in a word, even when everyone is seeking amusement, Akaky Akakievich gave himself up to no amusement whatever. No one could say they had ever seen him at any evening party. Having written to his heart’s content, he went to bed, smiling in advance at the thought of tomorrow: what would God send him to copy tomorrow? So flowed the peaceful life of a man who, with a salary of four hundred roubles, knew how to be content with his lot; and so it might have flowed on into deep old age, if it were not for the various calamities scattered along the road of life, not only for titular councillors, but even for privy, actual, court and every other kind of councillor, even those who never give anyone counsel or take any themselves.

There is in Petersburg a powerful enemy of all who receive a salary of four hundred roubles a year or thereabouts. This enemy is none other than our northern frost, although they do say it is very healthy. After eight in the morning, just at the hour when the streets fill with people going to their departments, it begins to give such strong and stinging flicks, indiscriminately, to every nose, that the poor clerks absolutely do not know where to put them. At this time, when even those in the highest posts have aching foreheads from the frost and tears coming to their eyes, the poor titular councillors are sometimes defenceless. All their salvation lies in running as fast as they can, in their skimpy little overcoats, across five or six streets, and then stamping their feet hard in the porter’s lodge until all their faculties and talents for official duties, frozen on the way, have thawed out. For some time Akaky Akakievich had begun to feel that he was being stung especially hard in the back and shoulder, although he tried to run across the legal distance as fast as he could. He began to wonder at last whether there were not some sins in his overcoat. Having examined it well at home, he discovered that in two or three places, namely on the back and the shoulders, it had become as thin as muslin; the cloth had worn so thin that one could see through it, and the lining had fallen apart. It must be said that Akaky Akakievich’s overcoat was also a target for the clerks’ mockery; they even took away from it the noble name of overcoat and called it a dressing gown. It really was strangely made: its collar grew smaller every year, because it went to patch the other parts. The patching did not show the tailor’s art and came out, indeed, baggy and ugly. Seeing how matters stood, Akaky Akakievich decided that the overcoat would have to be taken to Petrovich, a tailor who lived somewhere on the fourth floor up a back staircase, and who, in spite of his one blind eye and the pockmarks all over his face, did a pretty good business mending clerks’ and all sorts of other trousers and tailcoats; when he was sober, of course, and was not nursing some other enterprise in his head. About this tailor, of course, one ought not to say much, but since it is now the custom that in a story the character of every person must be fully described, there is nothing for it: let us have Petrovich here too. At first he was simply called Grigory and was a serf belonging to some gentleman; he began to call himself Petrovich from the time he got his freedom and began to drink rather heavily on every holiday, at first on the big ones, and then, without distinction, on all the church holidays, wherever there was a little cross in the calendar. In this respect he was faithful to the customs of his forefathers, and when quarrelling with his wife he would call her a worldly woman and a German. Since we have mentioned his wife, we must say a word or two about her too; but unfortunately not much was known about her, except that Petrovich had a wife, and that she even wore a cap and not a headscarf; but it seems she could not boast of beauty; at any rate, on meeting her only the soldiers of the Guards would peep under her cap, twitching their moustaches and making a peculiar sound.

Climbing the stairs that led to Petrovich’s, which, to do them justice, were all anointed with water and slops and soaked through and through with that alcoholic smell which stings the eyes and, as is well known, is ever present on all the back staircases of Petersburg houses; climbing the stairs, Akaky Akakievich was already wondering how much Petrovich would ask, and resolved in his mind not to give more than two roubles. The door was open, because the landlady, cooking some fish, had let so much smoke into the kitchen that one could not even see the cockroaches. Akaky Akakievich passed through the kitchen unnoticed even by the landlady herself, and came at last into the room, where he saw Petrovich sitting on a wide unpainted wooden table with his legs tucked under him like a Turkish pasha. His feet, as is the custom with tailors sitting at work, were bare. And the first thing that caught the eye was his big toe, very well known to Akaky Akakievich, with a deformed nail, thick and strong as a tortoise’s shell. Round Petrovich’s neck hung a skein of silk and thread, and on his knees lay some old rag. For about three minutes he had been trying to thread a needle, kept missing, and so was very angry with the darkness and even with the thread itself, grumbling under his breath: “It won’t go in, the savage; you’ve got the better of me, you rascal!” Akaky Akakievich was sorry to have come at exactly the moment when Petrovich was angry: he liked to give Petrovich orders when Petrovich was already somewhat in his cups, or, as his wife put it, “soaked in rotgut, the one-eyed devil”. In that state Petrovich usually gave way very readily and agreed, and even bowed and thanked him every time. Afterwards, it is true, his wife would come, weeping that her husband had been drunk and so had taken the job too cheaply; but one had only to add ten kopecks and the thing was settled. Now, however, Petrovich seemed to be sober, and therefore stiff, hard to deal with, and inclined to ask the devil knows what prices. Akaky Akakievich realised this and was about to beat a retreat, as they say, but the thing had already been begun. Petrovich screwed up his one eye at him very intently, and Akaky Akakievich involuntarily said:
“Good day, Petrovich!”
“Good day to you, sir,” said Petrovich, and squinted his eye at Akaky Akakievich’s hands, wanting to see what sort of booty he was carrying.
“Well, I’ve come to you, Petrovich, you know...”

It must be said that Akaky Akakievich expressed himself mostly in prepositions, adverbs and, finally, the kind of particles that have absolutely no meaning. And if the matter was very difficult, he even had the habit of not finishing his sentences at all, so that very often, having begun a speech with the words, “This, really, is altogether, you know...”, nothing more would follow, and he himself would forget, thinking he had said everything.

“What is it, then?” said Petrovich, and at the same time looked over his whole uniform with his one eye, from the collar to the sleeves, the back, the tails and the buttonholes, all of which was very familiar to him, since it was his own work. That is the custom with tailors: it is the first thing they do when they meet you.

“Well, I, you know, Petrovich... the overcoat, the cloth... you see, everywhere else it’s quite strong; it’s got a bit dusty and it looks as though it were old, but it’s new; only in one place it’s a little, you know... on the back, and here on one shoulder it’s worn a little, and on this shoulder a little; you see, that’s all. And it’s not much work...”

Petrovich took the dressing gown, spread it out first on the table, examined it for a long time, shook his head, and reached to the window sill for a round snuffbox with a portrait of some general on it, which general nobody knew, because the place where the face had been had been poked through with a finger and then pasted over with a square scrap of paper. Having taken a pinch of snuff, Petrovich held the dressing gown out at arm’s length, examined it against the light, and again shook his head. Then he turned it lining upwards and shook his head again; again he took the lid off the general with the paper pasted over him, stuffed his nose with snuff, closed the box, put it away, and at last said:
“No, it can’t be mended: it’s a wretched garment!”
At these words Akaky Akakievich’s heart sank.
“Why can’t it, Petrovich?” he said, almost in the pleading voice of a child. “It’s only worn a little on the shoulders; surely you have some bits of cloth...”
“Bits of cloth can be found, there’ll be bits,” said Petrovich, “but you can’t sew them on: the stuff is completely rotten; touch it with a needle and it just falls apart.”
“Let it fall apart, and you put a little patch on at once.”
“But there’s nothing to put the patch on; there’s nothing for it to hold on to; it’s too far gone. It’s cloth in name only; if the wind blew, it would fly to pieces.”
“Well, just fasten one on. How can it be like this, really, you know!..”

“No,” said Petrovich decisively, “nothing can be done. It’s in a very bad way. You’d better, when the cold winter weather comes, make yourself some foot-wrappings out of it, because a stocking doesn’t keep you warm. The Germans invented them so as to get more money for themselves” (Petrovich liked to have a dig at the Germans when he had the chance). “And as for the overcoat, it looks as if you’ll have to have a new one made.”

At the word “new” everything went misty before Akaky Akakievich’s eyes, and everything in the room began to swim before him. He saw clearly only the general with the face pasted over with paper on the lid of Petrovich’s snuffbox.
“A new one?” he said, still as if in a dream. “But I haven’t the money for that.”
“Yes, a new one,” said Petrovich with barbaric calm.
“Well, and if I had to have a new one, how much would it, you know...”
“You mean, what would it cost?”
“Yes.”

“You’d have to lay out three fifties and a bit more,” said Petrovich, and pressed his lips together significantly. He was very fond of strong effects; he liked to take someone completely aback somehow and then look sideways to see what face the person would make after such words.
“A hundred and fifty roubles for an overcoat!” cried poor Akaky Akakievich; cried, perhaps, for the first time in his life, for he was always distinguished by the quietness of his voice.
“Yes, sir,” said Petrovich, “and what an overcoat. If you put marten on the collar and add a hood with a silk lining, it’ll come to two hundred.”

“Petrovich, please,” said Akaky Akakievich in a pleading voice, not hearing and not trying to hear the words Petrovich had said and all his effects, “mend it somehow, so that it will serve a little longer at least.”
“Oh, no; that would be killing the work and wasting the money,” said Petrovich; and after these words Akaky Akakievich went out completely crushed.
And after he had gone, Petrovich stood for a long time with his lips pressed significantly together, not starting work, pleased that he had neither lowered himself nor betrayed the art of tailoring.

When he came out into the street, Akaky Akakievich was as if in a dream. “What a business, what a business,” he said to himself. “I really didn’t think it would turn out, you know...” and then, after some silence, he added: “So that’s how it is! So that’s what has come of it at last, and I really never could have supposed it would be like this.” Then followed another long silence, after which he said: “So that’s it! What a truly unexpected, you know... I would never have... such a circumstance!” Having said this, instead of going home he went in exactly the opposite direction, without suspecting it himself. On the way a chimney sweep brushed him with his whole sooty side and blackened his whole shoulder; a whole hatful of lime fell on him from the top of a house that was being built. He noticed none of this, and only later, when he bumped into a watchman who, having set his halberd beside him, was shaking snuff from a horn onto his calloused fist, did he come to himself a little, and only because the watchman said: “Why are you shoving right into my face? Haven’t you got the pavement?” This made him look round and turn towards home. Only here did he begin to collect his thoughts; he saw his position clearly and as it really was, and began to talk to himself, no longer in fragments but sensibly and frankly, as with a prudent friend with whom one can talk over a matter very close to one’s heart. “Well, no,” said Akaky Akakievich, “it’s no use talking to Petrovich now: he’s, you know... his wife must have given him a beating somehow. I’d better go to him on Sunday morning: after Saturday night he’ll be squinting and sleepy, so he’ll need a hair of the dog, and his wife won’t give him any money; and just then I’ll put ten kopecks, you know, into his hand; he’ll be more agreeable, and the overcoat then, you know...” So Akaky Akakievich reasoned with himself, cheered himself up, waited for the next Sunday, and, seeing from a distance that Petrovich’s wife was going out of the house somewhere, went straight to him. Petrovich was indeed squinting badly after Saturday, held his head towards the floor and was quite sleepy; but for all that, as soon as he learned what the matter was, it was as though the devil had nudged him. “It can’t be done,” he said. “Kindly order a new one.” It was then that Akaky Akakievich slipped him the ten kopecks. “Thank you kindly, sir; I’ll take a little something for your health,” said Petrovich, “and don’t you worry about the overcoat: it’s no good for anything. I’ll make you a new overcoat that will be a credit to us; we’ll stand by that.”

Akaky Akakievich tried again to say something about mending, but Petrovich did not hear him out and said: “I’ll make you a new one without fail, you may rely on that; we’ll do our best. We can even do it in the latest fashion: the collar will fasten with silver clasps under appliqué.”

It was then that Akaky Akakievich saw that he could not do without a new overcoat, and his spirits sank completely. How, indeed, with what, with what money could it be made? Of course, he could rely partly on the future holiday bonus, but that money had long ago been allotted and divided up in advance. He needed new trousers; he had to pay the cobbler an old debt for putting new uppers on old boot-legs; and he ought to order three shirts from the seamstress, and two of those undergarments which it is improper to name in print; in short, all the money was bound to go; and even if the director were so gracious as to award him forty-five or fifty roubles instead of the forty roubles bonus, there would still be only some trifle left, which in the capital needed for an overcoat would be a drop in the ocean. Although, of course, he knew that Petrovich had a whim of suddenly asking the devil knows what outrageous price, so that even his wife could not help crying out: “Are you out of your mind, you fool! Another time he’ll take a job for nothing, and now the devil has put it into him to ask a price he isn’t worth himself.” Although, of course, he knew that Petrovich would take the job on for eighty roubles; but even so, where could he get those eighty roubles? Half might be found: half could be found; perhaps even a little more; but where to get the other half?.. But first the reader must learn where the first half came from. Akaky Akakievich had the habit, out of every rouble he spent, of putting aside a kopeck into a little box, locked with a key, with a hole cut in the lid for dropping money in. At the end of every half year he would inspect the copper sum that had accumulated and exchange it for small silver. He had kept this up for a long time, and so in the course of several years the accumulated sum had come to more than forty roubles. So half was in hand; but where to get the other half? Where to get another forty roubles? Akaky Akakievich thought and thought, and decided that he would have to cut down his ordinary expenses, at least for one year: give up drinking tea in the evenings, not light a candle in the evenings, and if he needed to do anything, go into his landlady’s room and work by her candle; when walking in the streets, step as lightly and carefully as possible on the stones and flagstones, almost on tiptoe, so as not to wear out his soles too soon; send his linen to the laundress as rarely as possible, and so that it would not wear out, take it off every time he came home and stay in only his cotton dressing gown, very old and spared even by time itself. It must be told truthfully that at first it was somewhat hard for him to get used to such restrictions, but then he somehow got used to them and things went smoothly; he even became quite accustomed to going hungry in the evenings; but on the other hand he was nourished spiritually, carrying in his thoughts the eternal idea of the future overcoat. From then on it was as if his very existence had somehow become fuller, as if he had married, as if some other person were present with him, as if he were not alone but some pleasant companion of life had agreed to walk the road of life together with him; and this companion was none other than that same overcoat with thick wadding and a strong lining that would never wear out. He became somehow livelier, even firmer in character, like a man who has already defined and set himself a goal. Doubt and indecision disappeared of their own accord from his face and his actions; in a word, all wavering and indefinite traits. At times a fire showed in his eyes; the boldest and most daring thoughts even flashed through his head: why not, indeed, put marten on the collar? Thinking about it almost made him absent-minded. Once, while copying a paper, he very nearly made a mistake, so that he almost cried “Oh!” aloud and crossed himself. At least once every month he called on Petrovich to talk about the overcoat, where best to buy the cloth, and what colour, and at what price; and, though somewhat anxious, he always came home contented, thinking that the time would come at last when all this would be bought and the overcoat would be made. Things went even faster than he had expected. Contrary to all expectations, the director awarded Akaky Akakievich not forty or forty-five roubles, but a whole sixty; whether he had a presentiment that Akaky Akakievich needed an overcoat, or whether it just happened so, at any rate this left him with twenty roubles extra. This circumstance hastened matters. Another two or three months of a little hunger, and Akaky Akakievich had indeed saved about eighty roubles. His heart, generally very calm, began to beat. On the very first day he went with Petrovich to the shops. They bought very good cloth, and no wonder, since they had been thinking about it for half a year before, and hardly a month had gone by without their going into the shops to compare prices; so Petrovich himself said there was no better cloth to be had. For the lining they chose calico, but calico so sound and thick that, according to Petrovich, it was even better than silk, and even handsomer and glossier to look at. They did not buy marten, because it really was expensive; instead they chose cat, the best to be found in the shop, cat which from a distance could always be taken for marten. Petrovich spent only two weeks on the overcoat, because there was a great deal of quilting; otherwise it would have been ready sooner. Petrovich charged twelve roubles for the work; less was quite impossible: everything was sewn in silk, with a double fine seam, and afterwards Petrovich went over every seam with his own teeth, pressing various patterns into it. It was... it is hard to say on exactly which day, but probably on the most solemn day in the life of Akaky Akakievich, that Petrovich brought the overcoat at last. He brought it in the morning, just before the time when Akaky Akakievich had to leave for the department. At no other time could an overcoat have come more opportunely, because rather hard frosts were already beginning and seemed to threaten to grow harder still. Petrovich appeared with the overcoat as a good tailor should. His face wore an expression so significant that Akaky Akakievich had never seen anything like it. He seemed to feel to the full that he had done no small thing, and had suddenly revealed in himself the abyss that separates tailors who only put in linings and do alterations from those who make new garments. He took the overcoat out of the handkerchief in which he had brought it; the handkerchief had just come from the laundress, and afterwards he folded it and put it in his pocket for use. Having taken out the overcoat, he looked at it very proudly and, holding it in both hands, threw it very deftly over Akaky Akakievich’s shoulders; then he pulled it and smoothed it down at the back with his hand; then he draped it on Akaky Akakievich somewhat open in front. Akaky Akakievich, as a man of a certain age, wanted to try it with his arms in the sleeves; Petrovich helped him put it on with his arms in the sleeves, and it turned out that with the sleeves too it was good. In a word, it turned out that the overcoat fitted perfectly and exactly. Petrovich did not miss the opportunity to say that it was only because he lived without a signboard on a small street, and had besides known Akaky Akakievich for a long time, that he had charged so little; on Nevsky Prospect they would have charged him seventy-five roubles for the work alone. Akaky Akakievich did not want to discuss this with Petrovich, and was afraid besides of all the big sums with which Petrovich liked to throw dust in people’s eyes. He paid him, thanked him, and went out at once in his new overcoat to the department. Petrovich went out after him and, staying in the street, looked for a long time from a distance at the overcoat, and then deliberately went off to one side so that, cutting round by a crooked lane, he could run out into the street again and look at his overcoat once more from the other side, that is, straight in the face. Meanwhile Akaky Akakievich walked along in the most festive frame of mind. Every instant of every minute he felt that he had a new overcoat on his shoulders, and several times he even smiled from inner pleasure. Indeed, there were two advantages: one, that it was warm, and the other, that it was fine. He did not notice the road at all and found himself suddenly in the department; in the porter’s lodge he took off his overcoat, looked it all over, and entrusted it to the porter’s special care. Nobody knows how, but everyone in the department suddenly learned that Akaky Akakievich had a new overcoat and that the dressing gown no longer existed. At that very minute they all ran out to the porter’s lodge to look at Akaky Akakievich’s new overcoat. They began to congratulate him and greet him, so that at first he only smiled, and then he even began to feel ashamed. And when they all came up to him and began to say that the new overcoat must be wetted, and that at the very least he must give them all a party, Akaky Akakievich lost his head completely; he did not know what to do, what to answer, or how to get out of it. A few minutes later, blushing all over, he began quite simple-heartedly to assure them that it was not a new overcoat at all, that it was nothing, that it was an old overcoat. At last one of the clerks, an assistant head clerk no less, probably to show that he was not proud at all and mixed even with those beneath him, said: “Very well, I will give a party instead of Akaky Akakievich, and I invite you all to tea at my place today: as it happens, it’s my name day today.” The clerks, naturally, at once congratulated the assistant head clerk and accepted the invitation gladly. Akaky Akakievich began to make excuses, but they all began to say that it was impolite, that it was simply a shame and a disgrace, and he could not possibly refuse. Afterwards, though, he felt pleased when he remembered that it would give him the chance to walk out in his new overcoat even in the evening. That whole day was for Akaky Akakievich like the greatest solemn holiday. He came home in the happiest frame of mind, took off his overcoat and hung it carefully on the wall, admiring the cloth and the lining once more; and then, for comparison, he deliberately pulled out his former dressing gown, which had completely fallen apart. He looked at it and even laughed himself: such a vast difference! And for a long time afterwards, at dinner, he kept smiling whenever he thought of the state the dressing gown was in. He dined cheerfully, and after dinner he wrote nothing at all, no papers, but just played the sybarite a little on his bed until it grew dark. Then, without delaying, he dressed, put the overcoat on his shoulders, and went out into the street. Where exactly the clerk who had invited him lived, we regret we cannot say: our memory is beginning to fail us badly, and everything in Petersburg, all the streets and houses, have so blended and mixed together in our head that it is very hard to get anything out of it in decent order. Be that as it may, it is certain at least that the clerk lived in the best part of the town, and therefore very far from Akaky Akakievich. At first Akaky Akakievich had to pass through some deserted streets with scanty lighting, but as he came nearer to the clerk’s flat the streets became livelier, more crowded and more brightly lit. Pedestrians began to flash by more often; ladies began to appear, beautifully dressed; beaver collars could be seen on the men; there were fewer poor cabbies with their wooden latticed sledges studded with gilt nails; on the contrary, there were more and more smart drivers in raspberry velvet caps, with lacquered sledges and bearskin rugs, and carriages with ornamented boxes flew down the street, their wheels squealing on the snow. Akaky Akakievich looked at all this as at something new. For several years he had not gone out into the street in the evening. He stopped with curiosity in front of the lighted window of a shop to look at a picture of some beautiful woman taking off her shoe, thereby baring her whole leg, a very nice one; while behind her back, from the door of another room, a man with side-whiskers and a handsome little tuft of beard under his lip was poking his head out. Akaky Akakievich shook his head and smiled, and then went on his way. Why he smiled, whether because he had come across something completely unfamiliar to him, but of which everyone nevertheless keeps some sort of instinct, or whether he thought, like many other clerks, something like this: “Well, those French! What can one say! If they want something, you know, then it’s really, you know...” Or perhaps he did not even think that: after all, one cannot climb into a man’s soul and find out everything he thinks. At last he reached the house where the assistant head clerk lived. The assistant head clerk lived in grand style: a lantern shone on the stairs, and the flat was on the second floor. Going into the hall, Akaky Akakievich saw whole rows of galoshes on the floor. Among them, in the middle of the room, stood a samovar, humming and sending out clouds of steam. On the walls hung overcoats and cloaks, some of them even with beaver collars or velvet lapels. Beyond the wall one could hear noise and talk, which suddenly became clear and loud when the door opened and a footman came out with a tray of empty glasses, a cream jug and a basket of rusks. It was evident that the clerks had gathered long ago and had already drunk their first glass of tea. Akaky Akakievich, having hung up his overcoat himself, went into the room, and before him flashed all at once candles, clerks, pipes, card tables, and his ears were vaguely struck by the rapid talk rising on all sides and the noise of chairs being moved. He stopped very awkwardly in the middle of the room, looking about and trying to think what to do. But they had already noticed him, received him with a shout, and they all went out at once into the hall and looked over his overcoat again. Although Akaky Akakievich was somewhat embarrassed, being a simple-hearted man he could not help rejoicing to see how everyone praised the overcoat. Then, of course, they all abandoned both him and the overcoat and turned, as usual, to the tables set out for whist. All this, the noise, the talk and the crowd of people, was somehow strange to Akaky Akakievich. He simply did not know what to do, where to put his hands, his feet and his whole figure; at last he sat down by the players, looked at the cards, peered into one face and another, and after a while began to yawn and feel bored, all the more since the time when he usually went to bed had long since come. He wanted to say goodbye to the host, but they would not let him go, saying that he absolutely must drink a glass of champagne in honour of the new acquisition. An hour later supper was served, consisting of salad, cold veal, pâté, pastries and champagne. They made Akaky Akakievich drink two glasses, after which he felt that the room had become merrier; but he could not forget that it was already midnight and long past time to go home. So that the host should not somehow take it into his head to keep him, he left the room quietly, found his overcoat in the hall, which he saw, not without regret, lying on the floor, shook it, picked off every bit of fluff, put it on his shoulders and went down the stairs into the street. In the street it was still light. Some little shops, those permanent clubs of house servants and all sorts of people, were open; others, which were shut, still showed a long stream of light all along the crack of the door, showing that they were not yet without company, and that probably maids or menservants were still finishing their gossip and talk, leaving their masters in complete bewilderment as to where they were. Akaky Akakievich walked along in a cheerful frame of mind; he even suddenly began, nobody knows why, to run after some lady who passed by like lightning and every part of whose body was full of extraordinary movement. But he stopped at once and went on again very slowly as before, even wondering himself at the trot that had come from heaven knows where. Soon there stretched before him those deserted streets which are not very cheerful even in the daytime, still less in the evening. Now they had become even more remote and lonely: the street lamps began to flicker more rarely (less oil was evidently being supplied); wooden houses and fences began; nowhere a soul; only the snow glittered in the streets, and the low, sleeping hovels with their shutters closed showed sadly black. He came near the place where the street was cut across by an endless square with houses barely visible on its far side, which looked like a terrible desert.

Far away, God knows where, a light flickered in some watchman’s box which seemed to stand at the end of the world. Akaky Akakievich’s cheerfulness somehow diminished considerably here. He stepped out onto the square not without some involuntary fear, as though his heart had a presentiment of something bad. He looked back and to either side: it was just like a sea around him. “No, better not even look,” he thought, and walked on with his eyes closed; and when he opened them to see whether the end of the square was near, he suddenly saw standing in front of him, almost under his nose, some men with moustaches; who exactly, he could not even make out. Everything went misty before his eyes and his heart began to pound. “But that overcoat is mine!” said one of them in a voice like thunder, seizing him by the collar. Akaky Akakievich was about to shout “Help!” when the other put a fist the size of a clerk’s head right up to his mouth, adding: “Just you shout!” Akaky Akakievich felt only that they took the overcoat off him and gave him a kick with a knee, and he fell on his back in the snow and felt nothing more. A few minutes later he came to and got to his feet, but there was no one there. He felt that it was cold in that open space and that his overcoat was gone; he began to shout, but his voice seemed to have no intention of reaching the ends of the square. In despair, shouting without stopping, he set off running across the square straight to the box, beside which stood a watchman, leaning on his halberd and looking, it seemed, with curiosity, wanting to know what the devil a man was running towards him from a distance for, shouting. Akaky Akakievich, running up to him, began to shout in a breathless voice that he was asleep and was not watching anything, and did not see a man being robbed. The watchman answered that he had seen nothing; that he had seen two men stop him in the middle of the square, but had thought they were his friends; and that instead of scolding for nothing, he had better go to the inspector tomorrow, and the inspector would find out who had taken the overcoat. Akaky Akakievich ran home in complete disorder: the hair that he still had in small quantities on his temples and the back of his head was completely dishevelled; his side, his chest and his whole trousers were covered with snow. The old woman, his landlady, hearing a terrible knocking at the door, jumped hastily out of bed and, with a shoe on only one foot, ran to open the door, modestly holding her nightdress together at her breast with her hand; but when she opened it, she stepped back, seeing Akaky Akakievich in such a state. And when he told her what had happened, she threw up her hands and said that he must go straight to the district superintendent; that the local constable would cheat him, make promises and lead him a dance; that it was best to go straight to the superintendent, whom she even knew, because Anna, a Finnish woman who used to be her cook, now had a place as nanny at the superintendent’s; that she often saw him himself as he drove past their house; and that he went to church every Sunday and prayed, and at the same time looked cheerfully at everyone, and that therefore, by all appearances, he must be a kind man. Having heard this decision, Akaky Akakievich trudged sadly to his room; and how he spent the night there may be judged by anyone who can in the least imagine the position of another. Early in the morning he went to the superintendent’s; but they said he was asleep. He came at ten: again they said he was asleep. He came at eleven: they said the superintendent was not at home. He came at dinner time, but the clerks in the hall would not let him in and wanted to know at all costs on what business, and what need had brought him, and what had happened. So that at last Akaky Akakievich, for once in his life, wanted to show some character, and said flatly that he must see the superintendent himself in person, that they dare not keep him out, that he had come from his department on government business, and that if he made a complaint against them, they would see. The clerks dared not say anything against this, and one of them went to call the superintendent. The superintendent received the story of the robbery of the overcoat in an extremely strange way. Instead of paying attention to the main point of the matter, he began to question Akaky Akakievich: why was he coming home so late, and had he not been calling at some house of ill repute; so that Akaky Akakievich was completely embarrassed, and left him without knowing himself whether the matter of the overcoat would take its proper course or not. All that day he did not go to the office (the only time in his life). The next day he appeared all pale and in his old dressing gown, which had become still more pitiful. The story of the robbery of the overcoat, although there were clerks who did not miss the chance even here to laugh at Akaky Akakievich, nevertheless touched many. They decided at once to take up a collection for him, but collected the merest trifle, because the clerks had already spent a great deal, subscribing for the director’s portrait and for some book or other, at the suggestion of the head of the section, who was a friend of the author; so the sum turned out to be the merest trifle. Someone, moved by compassion, decided at least to help Akaky Akakievich with good advice, telling him not to go to the local constable, because, although it might happen that the constable, wishing to earn the approval of his superiors, would somehow find the overcoat, the overcoat would still remain with the police unless he could produce legal proof that it belonged to him; it would be best of all for him to apply to a certain important person; that the important person, by writing and communicating with the proper people, could make the matter go forward more successfully. There was nothing for it; Akaky Akakievich decided to go to the important person. What exactly the post of the important person was, and what it consisted of, has remained unknown to this day. It should be known that a certain important person had only recently become an important person, and until then had been an unimportant person. Even now, as a matter of fact, his position was not considered important in comparison with others still more important. But there will always be a circle of people for whom what is unimportant in the eyes of others is already important. However, he tried to increase his importance by many other means, namely: he introduced the rule that the lower clerks should meet him on the stairs when he arrived at the office; that no one should dare to come to him directly, but that everything should go in the strictest order: a collegiate registrar should report to a provincial secretary, the provincial secretary to a titular councillor or whoever it might be, and only in this way should a matter reach him. So it is in holy Russia: everything is infected with imitation; everyone mimics and apes his superior. They even say that a certain titular councillor, when he was made head of some small separate office, at once partitioned off a special room for himself, calling it the “audience chamber”, and put at the door some ushers with red collars and gold braid, who would take hold of the door handle and open it for everyone who came, though an ordinary writing desk could barely fit into the “audience chamber”. The manners and customs of the important person were solid and majestic, but not complicated. The main foundation of his system was strictness. “Strictness, strictness and strictness,” he used to say, and at the last word he usually looked very significantly into the face of the person he was speaking to. Though there was no reason for this, since the dozen clerks who made up the whole administrative mechanism of the office were in a proper state of fear as it was; seeing him from a distance, they would leave their work and wait standing at attention until their chief had passed through the room. His usual conversation with his subordinates rang with strictness and consisted almost entirely of three phrases: “How dare you? Do you know whom you are speaking to? Do you understand who is standing before you?” In his heart, however, he was a kind man, good to his colleagues and obliging; but the rank of general had completely turned his head. Having received the rank of general, he somehow got muddled, lost his way, and did not know at all how to behave. When he happened to be with his equals, he was still a proper man, a very decent man, in many respects even not a stupid man; but as soon as he happened to be in company where there were people even one rank below him, he was simply hopeless: he said nothing, and his position aroused pity, all the more since he himself felt that he could have spent the time incomparably better. In his eyes one could sometimes see a strong desire to join some interesting conversation and circle, but he was stopped by the thought: would this not be too much on his part, would it not be too familiar, and would he not lower his importance by it? And as a result of such reasoning he remained forever in the same silent state, uttering only now and then some monosyllabic sounds, and so he acquired the title of the most boring of men. It was to this important person that our Akaky Akakievich came; and he came at the most unfavourable time, very inopportunely for himself, though opportunely for the important person. The important person was in his study, talking very, very cheerfully with an old acquaintance and childhood friend who had recently arrived and whom he had not seen for several years. At this moment it was announced to him that someone called Bashmachkin had come. He asked abruptly: “Who is he?” They answered: “Some clerk.” “Ah! He can wait; this is not the time,” said the important man. Here it must be said that the important man was telling a downright lie: he had the time; he and his friend had long ago talked about everything and had for a long time been filling the conversation with very long silences, only patting each other lightly on the thigh and saying: “So it is, Ivan Abramovich!” “Just so, Stepan Varlamovich!” But for all that he told the clerk to wait, in order to show his friend, a man who had long been out of the service and had stayed too long at home in the country, how long clerks were kept waiting in his anteroom. At last, having talked his fill, and still more having been silent his fill, and having smoked a cigar in a very comfortable armchair with a reclining back, he seemed suddenly to remember, and said to his secretary, who had stopped at the door with papers to report: “Oh yes, I believe a clerk is standing out there; tell him he may come in.” Seeing Akaky Akakievich’s humble appearance and his old uniform, he turned to him suddenly and said: “What do you want?”, in an abrupt and firm voice which he had practised beforehand in his room, alone and in front of the mirror, a week before he received his present post and the rank of general. Akaky Akakievich had already felt the proper timidity in good time, became somewhat confused and, as well as he could, as far as the freedom of his tongue allowed, explained, adding even more often than usual the particle “you know”, that there had been an overcoat, completely new, and that now he had been robbed of it in an inhuman way, and that he was applying to him so that, by his intercession, he might somehow, you know, write to the chief of police or someone else and find the overcoat. The general, for some unknown reason, found such a way of addressing him too familiar.

“What, my dear sir,” he went on abruptly, “don’t you know the procedure? Where have you come to? Don’t you know how business is conducted? You should first have submitted a petition about this to the office; it would have gone to the head clerk, to the head of the section, then it would have been passed to the secretary, and the secretary would have brought it to me...”

“But, Your Excellency,” said Akaky Akakievich, trying to gather together all the small handful of presence of mind that he had, and feeling at the same time that he was sweating terribly, “I ventured to trouble Your Excellency because secretaries, you know... are an unreliable lot...”

“What, what, what?” said the important person. “Where did you get such spirit? Where did you get such ideas? What insubordination is this that has spread among young people against their chiefs and superiors!”

The important person, it seems, had not noticed that Akaky Akakievich was already over fifty. So that if he could be called a young man at all, it was only relatively, that is, in relation to someone who was already seventy.
“Do you know whom you are saying this to? Do you understand who is standing before you? Do you understand that, do you understand it? I am asking you.”

Here he stamped his foot, raising his voice to such a powerful note that even someone other than Akaky Akakievich would have been frightened. Akaky Akakievich simply froze, staggered, trembled all over and could not stand at all: if the porters had not run up at once to hold him, he would have flopped onto the floor; he was carried out almost motionless. And the important person, pleased that the effect had exceeded even his expectations, and completely intoxicated by the thought that his word could even deprive a man of his senses, glanced sideways at his friend to see how he was taking it, and saw, not without pleasure, that his friend was in a most uncertain state and was even beginning to feel afraid himself.

How he went down the stairs, how he came out into the street, Akaky Akakievich remembered nothing of that. He could not feel his arms or his legs. Never in his life had he been so badly hauled over the coals by a general, and a strange general at that. He walked through the blizzard that whistled in the streets, with his mouth open, stumbling off the pavements; the wind, as is the Petersburg custom, blew at him from all four sides, from every side street. In a moment it had given him a quinsy in his throat, and he got home unable to say a single word; he swelled up all over and took to his bed. So powerful a proper dressing-down can sometimes be! The very next day he had a high fever. Thanks to the generous assistance of the Petersburg climate, the illness progressed faster than could have been expected, and when the doctor came, he felt his pulse and could find nothing to do but prescribe a poultice, solely so that the patient should not be left without the beneficent help of medicine; and at the same time he announced that in a day and a half it would be certainly all up with him. After which he turned to the landlady and said: “And you, my good woman, don’t waste any time: order him a pine coffin right away, because an oak one will be too dear for him.” Whether Akaky Akakievich heard these words, so fatal for him, and if he heard them, whether they had a shattering effect on him, whether he grieved for his wretched life, none of this is known, because he was all the time in delirium and fever. Visions, each stranger than the last, kept appearing to him: now he saw Petrovich and ordered him to make an overcoat with some kind of traps for thieves, who seemed to him to be constantly under the bed, and he kept calling his landlady to pull a thief out from under the blanket; now he asked why his old dressing gown was hanging in front of him, when he had a new overcoat; now it seemed to him that he was standing before the general, listening to a proper dressing-down, and saying, “I am sorry, Your Excellency!”; now, at last, he even cursed, uttering the most terrible words, so that his old landlady even crossed herself, never in her life having heard anything of the kind from him, all the more since these words came straight after the words “Your Excellency”. After that he talked complete nonsense, so that nothing could be understood; one could only see that his disordered words and thoughts kept turning round one and the same overcoat. At last poor Akaky Akakievich gave up the ghost. Neither his room nor his belongings were sealed up, because, in the first place, there were no heirs, and in the second, very little was left to inherit, namely: a bundle of goose quills, a quire of white government paper, three pairs of socks, two or three buttons torn off his trousers, and the dressing gown already known to the reader. Who got all this, God knows: I confess that even the teller of this story did not take an interest. Akaky Akakievich was carted off and buried. And Petersburg was left without Akaky Akakievich, as if he had never been in it. There vanished and disappeared a being protected by no one, dear to no one, interesting to no one, who had not even attracted the attention of the naturalist, who never fails to stick a pin through an ordinary fly and examine it under the microscope; a being who meekly bore the mockery of the office and went down to his grave without any extraordinary event, but for whom, all the same, though just before the very end of his life, there flashed a bright visitor in the form of an overcoat, which brightened his poor life for a moment, and on whom misfortune afterwards fell just as unbearably as it has fallen on the kings and rulers of the world... A few days after his death a porter was sent to his flat from the department with orders for him to come at once: the chief, it was said, required him. But the porter had to return empty-handed, reporting that he could not come any more, and to the question “Why not?” he expressed himself in these words: “Well, he’s dead; they buried him three days ago.” In this way the department learned of Akaky Akakievich’s death, and the very next day a new clerk was already sitting in his place, much taller, and forming his letters not in such a straight hand, but much more slanting and crooked.

But who could have imagined that this was not yet all about Akaky Akakievich, that he was destined to live noisily for a few days after his death, as if in reward for a life that no one had noticed? But so it happened, and our poor story unexpectedly takes on a fantastic ending.

Rumours suddenly spread through Petersburg that near the Kalinkin Bridge, and much further afield, a dead man had begun to appear at night in the form of a clerk looking for some stolen overcoat, and, on the pretext of the stolen overcoat, pulling every kind of overcoat off every pair of shoulders, regardless of rank or title: cat-fur, beaver, wadded, raccoon, fox and bearskin coats; in a word, every kind of fur and skin that people have ever devised to cover their own. One of the clerks from the department saw the dead man with his own eyes and at once recognised Akaky Akakievich; but this filled him with such fear that he ran off as fast as his legs could carry him, and so could not get a good look; he only saw the other shake his finger at him from a distance. Complaints came in constantly from all sides that backs and shoulders, if only of titular councillors, but no, even of privy councillors themselves, were exposed to severe colds because of the nightly snatching of overcoats. The police were given orders to catch the dead man at all costs, dead or alive, and to punish him in the cruellest way as an example to others; and they very nearly succeeded. Namely, a watchman of some district in Kiryushkin Lane had actually seized the dead man by the collar at the very scene of the crime, as he was attempting to pull a frieze overcoat off some retired musician who in his day had played the flute. Having seized him by the collar, the watchman called out to two of his comrades, whom he told to hold him, while he himself reached into his boot for just one minute to take out his birch-bark snuffbox and refresh his nose, which had been frostbitten six times in his life; but the snuff must have been of a kind that even a dead man could not stand. Before the watchman, having closed his right nostril with his finger, had time to sniff half a handful up his left, the dead man sneezed so violently that he spattered all three of them right in the eyes. While they were raising their fists to rub them, the dead man vanished without a trace, so that they did not even know whether he had really been in their hands. From then on the watchmen became so afraid of dead men that they were even afraid to seize live ones, and only shouted from a distance, “Hey, you, go on your way!”; and the dead clerk began to appear even beyond the Kalinkin Bridge, causing no small fear to all timid people.

But we have completely forgotten a certain important person, who, in truth, was very nearly the cause of the fantastic turn taken by this, however, entirely true story. First of all, justice demands that we say that a certain important person, soon after poor Akaky Akakievich had left, thoroughly dressed down, felt something like regret. Compassion was not foreign to him; many good impulses were accessible to his heart, although his rank very often prevented them from showing. As soon as his visiting friend had left his study, he even began to think about poor Akaky Akakievich. And from then on almost every day he saw before him the pale Akaky Akakievich, who had not been able to stand an official dressing-down. The thought of him troubled him so much that a week later he even decided to send a clerk to him to find out how he was and whether he could in fact be helped somehow; and when he was told that Akaky Akakievich had died suddenly of a fever, he was even struck by it, heard the reproaches of his conscience, and was out of sorts all day. Wishing to distract himself somehow and forget the unpleasant impression, he went to an evening party at a friend’s, where he found decent company and, best of all, almost everyone there was of the same rank, so that he could not be constrained by anything at all. This had an amazing effect on his state of mind. He opened up, became pleasant in conversation, amiable; in a word, he spent the evening very pleasantly. At supper he drank two glasses of champagne, a remedy which, as is well known, works not badly in the matter of cheerfulness. The champagne disposed him to various extravagances, namely: he decided not to go home yet, but to call on a lady he knew, Karolina Ivanovna, a lady, it seems, of German origin, towards whom he felt entirely friendly relations. It must be said that the important person was no longer a young man, a good husband and a respectable father of a family. Two sons, one of whom was already serving in an office, and a pretty sixteen-year-old daughter with a slightly turned-up but charming little nose, came every day to kiss his hand, saying “*Bonjour, papa.*” His wife, still a fresh woman and not at all bad-looking, would first give him her hand to kiss and then, turning it over, kiss his hand. But the important person, though entirely satisfied with domestic family tenderness, found it proper to have a lady friend for friendly relations in another part of the town. This lady friend was not a bit better or younger than his wife; but such puzzles exist in the world, and it is not for us to judge them. And so the important person came down the stairs, got into his sledge and said to the coachman: “To Karolina Ivanovna’s”; and he himself, wrapped very luxuriously in a warm overcoat, remained in that pleasant state than which nothing better can be imagined for a Russian, that is, when you are not thinking of anything yourself, and meanwhile thoughts come into your head of their own accord, each pleasanter than the last, without even giving you the trouble of chasing after them and looking for them. Full of pleasure, he lightly recalled all the merry moments of the evening, all the words that had made the little circle roar with laughter; many of them he even repeated under his breath and found that they were just as funny as before, and so it is no wonder that he laughed heartily himself. Now and then, however, he was bothered by a gusty wind, which, bursting out suddenly from God knows where and for no known reason, cut right into his face, throwing bits of snow into it, flapping his overcoat collar like a sail, or suddenly, with unnatural force, throwing it over his head, and so giving him endless trouble getting out of it. Suddenly the important person felt that someone had seized him very firmly by the collar. Turning round, he saw a short man in an old, worn uniform, and recognised him, not without horror, as Akaky Akakievich. The clerk’s face was white as snow and looked like that of a dead man. But the horror of the important person went beyond all bounds when he saw the dead man’s mouth twist and, breathing on him the terrible smell of the grave, utter these words: “Ah! So here you are at last! At last I have, you know, caught you by the collar! It’s your overcoat I need! You didn’t trouble about mine, and you dressed me down besides; so now give me yours!” The poor important person almost died. However much character he showed in the office and in general before his subordinates, and although everyone who looked at his manly appearance and figure said, “Oh, what a character!”, here, like very many people of heroic appearance, he felt such fear that he even began, not without reason, to be afraid of some sort of fit. He even threw off his overcoat from his shoulders himself as fast as he could, and shouted to the coachman in a voice not his own: “Home, at full speed!” The coachman, hearing the voice that is usually used at decisive moments and is even accompanied by something much more effective, hunched his head into his shoulders just in case, raised his whip, and flew off like an arrow. In a little over six minutes the important person was already at the door of his own house. Pale, terrified and without his overcoat, instead of going to Karolina Ivanovna’s he had come home; he dragged himself somehow to his room and spent the night in very great disorder, so that the next morning at tea his daughter said to him straight out: “You are quite pale today, Papa.” But Papa said nothing and told no one a word about what had happened to him, or where he had been, or where he had wanted to go. This incident made a strong impression on him. He even began to say to his subordinates much less often, “How dare you? Do you understand who is standing before you?”; and if he did say it, it was not until he had first heard what the matter was about. But even more remarkable is that from then on the appearances of the dead clerk stopped entirely: the general’s overcoat must have fitted his shoulders perfectly; at any rate, no more such cases of overcoats being snatched from anyone were heard of anywhere. However, many active and solicitous people would not calm down at all, and kept saying that the dead clerk was still appearing in the outlying parts of the town. And indeed, a watchman in Kolomna saw with his own eyes a ghost appear from behind a house; but being by nature somewhat feeble, so that once an ordinary full-grown piglet, rushing out of some private house, knocked him off his feet, to the great amusement of the cabmen standing around, from whom he demanded a farthing each for snuff for such mockery; and so, being feeble, he did not dare to stop it, but followed it in the darkness until at last the ghost suddenly looked round and, stopping, asked: “What do you want?”, and showed a fist such as you will not find even among the living. The watchman said, “Nothing,” and turned back at once. The ghost, however, was much taller, wore an enormous moustache, and, directing its steps, it seemed, towards the Obukhov Bridge, vanished completely into the darkness of the night.
